title: Careful words (Avot 1:9)
hook: Simeon ben Shetach: question witnesses well, and guard your words so no one learns to lie
carry: a question can teach a lie

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nittai of Arbel: keep far from a bad neighbor, and don't give up on justice. Your line was choose your neighbors. Did you step back from one bad influence? Day two hundred forty-one.

A kid is standing in the kitchen with crumbs on his shirt, and a parent asks, you didn't take the last cookie, did you? And the kid, who is not a fool, says no. Notice what happened. The question handed him the answer. It told him which story would get him out of trouble. Questions like that get asked at home, at work, in a group chat. Long ago, a judge in Jerusalem noticed the same thing in a courtroom, where the stakes were a lot higher than a cookie. Today: careful words.
screen: `CRUMBS ON HIS SHIRT.` → `THE QUESTION HANDED HIM THE ANSWER.` → `A JUDGE IN JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: The judge is Simeon ben Shetach, who with his partner Judah ben Tabbai makes up one of the pairs of teachers in the chain of Pirkei Avot. He led the court in a stormy time, and later tradition remembers him as fearless in front of kings. His saying, in chapter one, comes in two halves. First: examine the witnesses thoroughly. The Torah says a matter is established by two or three witnesses, and Simeon wants them questioned hard, because a careless court convicts the innocent. Then the second half, which is the surprising one: and be careful with your words, so that they don't learn from them to lie. That half isn't aimed at the witnesses. It's aimed at the judge. If the judge asks, was the knife in his right hand, the witness now knows the court is looking for a knife in a right hand. The question teaches the lie. So the careful judge asks open questions, and lets the story come out on its own. The Talmud tells a story about Simeon that shows how seriously he took this. He once saw a man chase another man into a ruin. He ran in after them and found one man dying and the other holding a bloody sword. And Simeon said, in effect: either you killed him, or I did. But I can't convict you. The Torah needs two witnesses, and I only saw the sword, not the blow. Even when he was sure, he held himself to the court's rule. That's the idea for today. Our questions shape what people tell us, and what we say we saw becomes someone else's truth.
screen: `SIMEON BEN SHETACH, A JUDGE.` · `QUESTION THE WITNESSES WELL.` · `YOUR QUESTION CAN TEACH THE LIE.` · `THE SWORD IN THE RUIN.` · then, large: `CAREFUL WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse one open question. Settle, and breathe. Think of a conversation you'll have today where you want the truth. With a child, a coworker, a friend. Notice the question you'd normally ask, the one with the answer tucked inside it. Now, slowly, turn it into an open one. Not, you finished it, right? Just, how did it go? Say it silently a few times, until it feels natural. The bell holds the time.
Careful words. Simeon ben Shetach's warning to judges: the way you ask can teach someone how to lie.
Your line: a question can teach a lie. Today, when you want to know what really happened, ask an open question and then stop talking. Day two hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Jewish law built strict rules for testimony on this teaching: witnesses are questioned separately and closely, and Avot 1:9 is also read as a guide to honest speech well beyond the courtroom.

original.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: be careful with your words.

trapdoor: what it means: a judge's questions can teach a witness how to lie, so ask with care.
what a scholar hears: some classic commentators read the warning as addressed to the judge, whose leading questions shape the testimony.

notes: Avot is paraphrased throughout (the outline follows Taylor 1897, which is public domain but not on the validator's list).
The story of the man with the bloody sword is told of Simeon ben Shetach in Sanhedrin 37b and Shevuot 34a (and in the Mekhilta); confirm the attribution and the paraphrase.
Dating Simeon ben Shetach to the first century BCE and 'fearless in front of kings' (Sanhedrin 19a, the story with King Yannai): confirm.
The reading that the second clause is aimed at the judge follows commentators such as Bartenura; confirm.
